claims.text: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered single-phase BCC high-entropy alloy.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa.
The limited plasticity of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is attributable to its high Mo content and the associated electronegativity landscape.
Tungsten is similarly refractory to molybdenum.
Replacing roughly 20% of the Mo atoms with W can preserve the alloy's disordered BCC structure.
Partial replacement of Mo by W will reduce the alloy's overall electronegativity difference.
W substitution will reduce local bonding heterogeneity and produce a more uniformly bonded lattice.
Reduced electronegativity disparity and bonding heterogeneity will lower resistance to dislocation motion.
Lower resistance to dislocation motion will improve room-temperature compressive plasticity.
The atomic size and modulus of W will preserve intrinsic strengthening through lattice distortion.
Moderate W substitution will increase compressive plastic strain relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
The W-modified alloy will retain a compressive yield strength close to 1719 MPa.
The beneficial effect is limited to no more than approximately 30% replacement of the Mo atoms by W.
Excessive W substitution could cause phase segregation or loss of strength.
Maintaining a single disordered BCC phase is required for the proposed strength–plasticity benefit.

contradictions.description: The boundary only predicts benefit somewhere within a moderate substitution regime, whereas the falsification rule says that failure of any single composition up to 30% replacement falsifies the hypothesis. Thus, one nonoptimal composition would falsify a claim that otherwise allows composition dependence and an unknown optimum.
